Last spring, someone painted the bench at the end of our street a blue so bright it made the sky look undecided. Nobody knew who had done it. The city benches were green, and the city, when asked, said it had no plans to change that.

For a week there was a sheet of cardboard on the seat with WET PAINT written in pencil. By Thursday, rain had erased the W, and people began sitting on it.

I started taking my coffee there before work. At seven fifteen, a woman in slippers walked a dog that refused to pass the storm drain. She had to pick him up, all forty pounds of him, and carry him the length of a sidewalk square. Once he was safely past, he trotted ahead as though the delay had been her idea.

In June, the city painted the bench green again. The painter missed a spot beneath the left armrest. You could still see the blue if you dropped something and had to crouch to get it.

A few weeks later, I came out with my coffee and found the woman sitting there. The dog was at her feet. She had one slipper on. The other lay beside the storm drain, just beyond the reach of his leash.

“Would you mind?” she asked.

I brought it over. She thanked me, put it on, and moved her bag so I could sit. Neither of us had anywhere to be for another ten minutes, so we stayed.
